live.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
live.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL: a threat actor tracked under many names
live.in_short: NICKEL KIMBALL is the Secureworks name for an actor also known as Kimsuky and APT43. The catalogue lists its aliases and tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL KIMBALL is the name Secureworks uses for this threat actor.
Other vendors track it under many other names, including APT43, Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, Velvet Chollima, THALLIUM, TA427 and Black Banshee.
The catalogue lists eight tools tied to the actor: BabyShark, FastFire, FastSpy, FireViewer, KONNI, KimJongRAT, Kimsuky and ReconShark.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
next.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL (Kimsuky): a long-running espionage cluster aimed mainly at South Korean targets
next.in_short: NICKEL KIMBALL, widely tracked as Kimsuky or APT43, is linked by several vendors to North Korea. Reports describe phishing, shortcut-file and macro lures, and Android spyware, mostly aimed at South Korean targets.

sentences.t: Secureworks tracks this actor as NICKEL KIMBALL. Other vendors use names such as Kimsuky, APT43, Velvet Chollima, Black Banshee, THALLIUM, Emerald Sleet and TA427.
Breakglass Intelligence attributes Kimsuky (which it lists as APT43, Velvet Chollima and Black Banshee) to North Korea with high confidence.
ESRC, a South Korean malware analysis team, describes Thallium (also known as Kimsuky) as a North Korea-linked threat.

Sekoia and Kudelski Security note that some DPRK experts regard Kimsuky as a mega-cluster made up of several branches, such as TA406 and TA408. The report adds that vendors name and divide clusters differently.

Genians Security Center assesses with moderate confidence that Kimsuky ran a campaign against South Korean policy and security professionals, using reply-based spearphishing that posed as a National Assembly member's aide.

According to South Korea's National Police Agency, Kimsuky exploited an email server flaw at a defense subcontractor between April and July 2023. The flaw let large files be downloaded without authentication.
AhnLab's ASEC team reported signs of AppleSeed, a backdoor it says Kimsuky mainly uses, being spread to maintenance contractors of a military unit in July 2022.
Breakglass Intelligence reports phishing lures aimed at South Korean Naver users.

AhnLab reports that Kimsuky uses spear-phishing emails with shortcut files disguised as normal documents. The chain then uses PowerShell, scheduled tasks, and a Dropbox and TCP socket command channel.
AhnLab also describes a patched system DLL used to disable Remote Desktop authentication. It says the group has moved away from the open-source RDP Wrapper it used before.
ASEC describes a password-protected Excel file with a macro that asks the user to enable content. The macro then fetches a further script that installs AppleSeed.

Breakglass Intelligence describes a three-stage chain that starts from a compiled help file disguised as API documentation. It ends in a keylogger with clipboard monitoring and timed data exfiltration.

ENKI WhiteHat attributes new Android DOCSWAP variants to Kimsuky, citing shared infrastructure, a known phishing string and Korean-language comments. It says the apps carry a RAT with keylogging through the Accessibility Service.
S2W first named DocSwap and suspects a possible connection to Kimsuky. It tracks the actor as puNK-004.
A technical blog says Kimsuky uses a persistence trick that hijacks the default file association for text files.

In April 2024, South Korea's National Police Agency warned that Lazarus, Andariel and Kimsuky had breached South Korean defense companies and their subcontractors to steal technology data. It said some firms had been compromised since late 2022 without knowing it.
AhnLab reported a PebbleDash backdoor distribution by Kimsuky in March 2025. The report says CISA earlier tied the backdoor to Lazarus, and that Kimsuky has used it since 2021.

Genians Security Center describes a campaign from June to October 2026 that used a Node.js remote access tool called NodeLinkRAT. Later stages were fetched from a public note service whose contents the operator swapped. Genians assesses it as Kimsuky, with moderate confidence.
Breakglass Intelligence, in a report dated 11 April 2026, mapped about 79 domains across five IPs tied to a Kimsuky command server.
Treat shortcut files, help files and macro-enabled documents that arrive by email as suspect, even when they look like ordinary paperwork.
Install Android apps only from trusted sources, and be wary of apps that ask for accessibility permissions.
